0fdc5427-4be3-59d8-9f17-1d7fc20d515a.blurb: A completed individual coding round featuring six original problems and a published editorial.
0fdc5427-4be3-59d8-9f17-1d7fc20d515a.description:
CodeCurrent brought students together for a three-hour online contest built around six original algorithmic problems. The set moved from approachable simulation to graph search, interval reasoning and a demanding dynamic programming finale. Participants chose their language, worked independently and used the live scoreboard to judge when to switch problems. Each accepted solution counted toward a standard penalty-based ranking, making efficient debugging just as valuable as recognizing the right algorithm.

This detail page is an archive of the 26 September round. Registration has closed and the recorded seats represent verified individual competitors, but the problem statements and editorial remain available through the participant portal. The post-contest discussion traced why several tempting greedy approaches failed and how to construct smaller counterexamples. If you attended, your final score and certificate can be requested from the contest desk; if you are exploring future rounds, the archived set offers a realistic sample of the difficulty. Prizes were based on the frozen, plagiarism-reviewed standings rather than the provisional scoreboard.

cb79e7f0-c9fc-55a0-9fa5-e348b8ce64d3.name: Between Lectures: Campus Photo Walk
cb79e7f0-c9fc-55a0-9fa5-e348b8ce64d3.blurb: Find the unnoticed stories of a campus morning through a three-image photo essay.
cb79e7f0-c9fc-55a0-9fa5-e348b8ce64d3.description:
Between Lectures invited student photographers to slow down and look at the places usually passed in a hurry: a half-open workshop door, a gardener arranging tools, a shadow crossing an empty corridor. The September walk paired a brief discussion of visual ethics with ninety minutes of observation around the campus. Participants used phones or cameras to build a three-image essay responding to the prompt “Work before the crowd arrives.”

After the walk, everyone selected and captioned their photographs in the media lab before a small-group critique. The contest rewarded a clear sequence and careful attention to context, rather than costly equipment or dramatic edits. This completed event page preserves the original route, submission rules and programme so future participants can understand the format. Entries were captured during the designated walk window, with permission requested for recognisable portraits. The afternoon showcase gave each photographer a chance to explain one creative decision and see how classmates told entirely different stories along the same familiar paths.

f4a7eca2-0363-5f01-96d8-40b80e7d3798.blurb: Learn a careful repair workflow for a torn backpack, loose button or low-voltage gadget with a tired connection.
f4a7eca2-0363-5f01-96d8-40b80e7d3798.description:
Before you replace a useful object, find out whether a small repair can give it another semester. This campus repair café pairs practical demonstrations with supervised work on simple personal items: a backpack seam, a loose button, a detached zip pull or a battery-powered gadget with an obvious connector fault. The session begins by separating safe beginner repairs from jobs that need a qualified professional. You will learn to inspect the damage, choose the smallest effective intervention and record what you changed so a later repair is easier.

Bring one eligible item and work through a repair plan with a facilitator before touching tools. Sewing and basic low-voltage inspection stations share a common goal: learning a repeatable process, even when the item cannot be restored. Mains appliances, swollen batteries and devices holding sensitive personal data are outside the café’s scope. Consumables are provided, but replacement parts are limited and success is not guaranteed. The registration list is already closed so the organisers can match each submitted item to suitable tools and supervision; confirmed participants should check their item approval email before arriving.

4819d0b0-4b31-527d-ab30-44cf58ed3b11.blurb: Tune a compact robot for junctions, sharp bends and a timed autonomous finish.
4819d0b0-4b31-527d-ab30-44cf58ed3b11.description:
TrackTact turns a strip of black tape into an engineering puzzle. Your autonomous robot will navigate a white arena with sharp turns, interrupted segments and marked junctions, using onboard sensing rather than a remote operator. The practice track shows the same obstacle types as the scored course, but the final sequence remains hidden until your run. Smooth recovery, reliable junction decisions and clean construction matter as much as top speed.

Teams start with a technical inspection and a short calibration slot before two timed qualification runs. The best valid time advances to the final, where a changed course tests whether your approach generalizes. A marshal will explain every time penalty before you enter the arena, and the pit area provides tables and mains sockets for careful repairs. Bring a robot you understand well enough to troubleshoot under pressure, not just a finished chassis. Beginners are welcome if they have tested basic line following; the event is a competition rather than an assembly workshop, and organizers cannot supply missing sensors or batteries.

6dac7dc2-0d4a-5688-b6bb-323e58d07757.name: SpanCraft: Lightweight Bridge Challenge
6dac7dc2-0d4a-5688-b6bb-323e58d07757.blurb: Build a 40-centimetre bridge from a fixed kit, then watch its strength-to-weight ratio tested.
6dac7dc2-0d4a-5688-b6bb-323e58d07757.description:
SpanCraft puts structural judgement on the table with a simple question: how much can a light bridge carry? Teams receive identical packs of wooden craft sticks, thread and fast-setting adhesive, then design a bridge for a clear 40-centimetre span. The structure must leave space for a central loading plate and remain within the published deck width and height limits. The winning design balances mass, load path and careful joints rather than simply using the largest amount of material.

The morning begins with a kit check and a demonstration of the loading rig. You then sketch, build and weigh your bridge before a shared curing window. In the afternoon, technicians add load in controlled steps while a screen displays the measured deflection and current weight. Teams explain one design decision before testing and receive a photograph of their bridge at the rig for later documentation. You do not need structural analysis software, but you should arrive ready to calculate, cut safely and revise a joint that does not work. Expect an energetic competition where the final failure can be as informative as a successful load test.

721c1a93-4118-56e8-8cb1-724ef7462243.blurb: Decode a food-delivery journey and redesign the moment where confused users abandon their order.
721c1a93-4118-56e8-8cb1-724ef7462243.description:
Why does a checkout flow feel effortless in one app and exhausting in another? This hands-on product lab studies a fictional food-delivery service from the first search to the final order confirmation. You will trace the customer journey, spot confusing choices and examine how delivery charges, empty states and error messages shape trust. The facilitator introduces a simple teardown method that connects screen-level decisions to user goals, business constraints and measurable outcomes, rather than asking you to judge an interface by how fashionable it looks.

Working in pairs for discussion, you will independently produce an annotated journey map and redesign one troublesome step in Figma or on paper. A short critique asks you to defend the change using a user story, an accessibility consideration and a sensible metric. No prior design portfolio is needed, and the supplied screens use invented brands and data. You leave with a compact case-study outline you can develop further, plus a checklist for analysing other products without mistaking personal preference for research.

3e0a5c84-eedf-507e-a9e8-3db7a70f9371.blurb: Two artists, one square and a pattern that turns a campus walkway into a shared story.
3e0a5c84-eedf-507e-a9e8-3db7a70f9371.description:
Chowk & Colour invites pairs to create a rangoli that draws people in from the edges and rewards a closer look. The theme “Water, Memory, Tomorrow” can become a river motif, a story of a village well, a geometric exploration of rainfall or another interpretation you can explain in your own words. Each duo works inside a marked one-and-a-half-metre square, making composition and teamwork as important as fine detail.

A common palette of dry colours gives every pair the same starting materials, while participants may bring approved natural additions such as petals, grains or leaves. You will have two hours to build the work, followed by a short explanation to the jury. The designs remain on view through the afternoon so visitors can follow the little exhibition along the sheltered walkway. Bring a plan, but leave room to adapt it to the space and texture of the floor; the most memorable rangoli is one in which the pattern and the story hold together.

a3e42d20-6d43-5a11-bb14-e25b6f3ea2d1.blurb: Watch a black-and-white image appear in the tray and make your first contact sheet and photographic print.
a3e42d20-6d43-5a11-bb14-e25b6f3ea2d1.description:
Digital photographs arrive instantly; this lab asks you to slow down and see how light becomes an image on paper. Working from supplied black-and-white negatives, you will make a contact sheet, select one frame and produce a small print under the enlarger. The facilitator explains aperture, exposure time, contrast filters and the difference between a correct exposure and the print you actually want. You will use test strips to make decisions rather than guessing at a full sheet of paper.

The group rotates through supervised stations so everyone handles an enlarger and observes the developer, stop bath and fixer sequence. Safety and access are part of the session: the darkroom uses low light, wet work areas and photographic chemicals, with gloves and ventilation provided. You will not develop a personal roll in this introductory workshop, because the schedule is built around learning a repeatable printing process. Leave with one contact sheet, one dry print and notes on how you reached it, including an honest record of the tests that did not work.

A marked warm-up zone and sprung practice mats are available before your slot, and the host keeps a visible clock for every performance. Register with a complete roster, submit clean audio in advance, and bring comfortable shoes: this is an evening built around movement, mutual respect and an audience close enough to feel every beat.

A missed bus connection, an inaccessible footpath or a confusing waste collection schedule can shape an entire day. CivicForge 24 asks teams to choose one everyday urban problem and build a practical response in a continuous 24-hour sprint. The opening brief includes fictional service data, resident interview excerpts and clearly scoped challenge tracks for mobility, accessibility and neighbourhood services. You can build an app, a dashboard, a hardware mock-up or a low-tech service prototype; judges will care about the problem you solve and the evidence behind your choices.

After the evening kickoff, teams settle into the Innovation Lab with mentor checkpoints, a midnight usability clinic and a quiet rest room nearby. The next afternoon, you will demonstrate a working slice of your idea, explain its limits and show how a resident would use it. Bring a team that enjoys testing assumptions as much as writing code. 42ba467c-d16a-5498-bcf2-f527bc29f957.blurb: Build a document-search assistant that cites its evidence and admits when the handbook has no answer.
42ba467c-d16a-5498-bcf2-f527bc29f957.description:
Build an assistant that answers from a college handbook instead of inventing campus rules. This lab follows the full retrieval-augmented generation workflow: prepare a small document collection, split it into useful passages, create embeddings, retrieve evidence and return an answer with citations. The teaching material includes deliberately ambiguous questions so you can see why a fluent response is not enough. You will inspect retrieved passages and compare simple keyword search with vector retrieval before connecting the results to a language model.

The afternoon focuses on failure modes that matter in a real student help desk: missing evidence, conflicting policy versions, unsafe instructions inside documents and requests for personal information. You will build a small evaluation set and add a clear fallback when the assistant cannot support an answer. A starter notebook and facilitator-managed model endpoint keep the lab approachable; no paid API account is required. Bring basic Python skills and expect to leave with a working local demonstration, an evaluation checklist and a better understanding of what your prototype can responsibly claim.

78401373-ca0f-5f0e-b00c-93bb4e2212ec.blurb: Train, evaluate and explain a model on a fictional multilingual campus helpdesk dataset.
78401373-ca0f-5f0e-b00c-93bb4e2212ec.description:
A useful AI model needs more than a high leaderboard score. In ModelMosaic, teams work with a supplied synthetic dataset of campus helpdesk questions in English, Hindi and Marathi, then build a classifier that routes requests to the right support desk. The challenge rewards macro-F1, clear treatment of uncertain predictions and evidence that performance does not collapse on less common language groups. A starter notebook and baseline make the task approachable without hiding the decisions that matter.

The online round opens with a data walkthrough and a discussion of leakage, label ambiguity and responsible reporting. During the six-hour build, you can compare classical models with small language models, inspect errors and decide when your system should ask for clarification. Finalists submit reproducible code and a short model card, then join a live screen-share review. This is a compact chance to practise the evaluation habits that turn an impressive experiment into a defensible product. GPU access is optional; an efficient CPU baseline can compete, and the organizers do not provide paid API credits.

9f14bfb9-e3ea-54ec-afdf-a1f07d8d17dd.blurb: Defend a surprise motion with clear reasoning, sharp rebuttal and a partner who can build the case with you.

Motion to Speak is a two-person parliamentary debate tournament for student speakers who enjoy thinking on their feet. The event uses a simplified Asian parliamentary format: two teams face off in each room, with government proposing the motion and opposition challenging it. Preliminary rounds draw from education, culture, technology and public life; specialised policy knowledge is less valuable than a clear argument and a fair response to the other side.

Every team receives three preliminary rounds and a short adjudicator debrief, so a first-round loss does not end your day. The top four teams advance to semifinals, followed by a public final. A briefing explains speaker order, points of information and the scoring rubric before the opening draw. You do not need a polished accent or prior championship experience. You do need to listen, distinguish facts from assumptions and make your partner’s contribution stronger. Bring a notebook, a water bottle and the confidence to revise your case when a good challenge lands.

f326be50-5933-5d50-b03b-86270f238b1e.blurb: Guide a small protected quadcopter through a marshalled indoor obstacle course.
f326be50-5933-5d50-b03b-86270f238b1e.description:
RotorRush is a controlled indoor flying challenge built around precision rather than altitude. Two-person teams bring a small quadcopter with full propeller guards, then navigate a netted course of hoops, gates and a marked landing pad. One student pilots while the other acts as a spotter and keeps track of the route. The timed run rewards a clean path and a stable landing; shortcuts, missed gates and contact with obstacles add clearly published penalties.

Before anyone flies, the arena team checks aircraft dimensions, battery condition, failsafe behaviour and the emergency disarm procedure. Every squad receives a supervised familiarization flight, followed by two scored attempts. Only one aircraft is active inside the enclosure at a time, and spectators remain behind a separate barrier. This is an indoor model-flight competition, with no outdoor campus flying or aerial photography permitted. Bring a machine you can handle confidently at low speed and a teammate who communicates clearly. There is a charging table under staff supervision, but spare charged batteries are strongly recommended to keep the programme moving.

2debc524-b43f-54c5-affd-5246f57a51e7.name: Lines in Motion: Live Illustration Jam
2debc524-b43f-54c5-affd-5246f57a51e7.blurb: Turn a live movement session into one expressive illustration in ninety minutes.
2debc524-b43f-54c5-affd-5246f57a51e7.description:
Lines in Motion asks illustrators to notice how a gesture changes before trying to capture it. A student movement ensemble offers a sequence of brief poses, a longer held tableau and a final improvised passage. You can translate what you see into expressive figures, abstract shapes, sequential panels or a composition that follows rhythm rather than literal anatomy. The final work should show a considered response to the live source.

The jam begins with a non-scored warm-up on scrap paper, giving everyone time to settle their tools and test the view from their seat. The ninety-minute competition then combines short observation intervals with quiet drawing time; the model sequence is repeated so no one has to rely on a single glimpse. Participants choose traditional media or an offline digital tablet, and the completed works appear together in a small studio display. Bring a medium you know well, protect the shared tables, and be ready to explain one mark that made your drawing come alive.

6aa44f45-fdd2-56a9-a05c-f64dba85bf40.name: Seed Stage: The Campus Venture Pitch
6aa44f45-fdd2-56a9-a05c-f64dba85bf40.blurb: Turn a tested campus problem into a six-minute pitch, a credible business case and your next customer conversation.
6aa44f45-fdd2-56a9-a05c-f64dba85bf40.description:
You have found a problem that people complain about every week. Can you show that they will pay for a better answer? Seed Stage brings student ventures into a working pitch room, where teams explain the customer, demonstrate the proposed solution and defend the numbers behind their first year. Ideas in education, climate, consumer services and campus life are welcome; a polished app is optional, but evidence from at least five customer conversations is required. A short application screens for clarity rather than company registration or prior funding.

Selected teams receive a deck template and a rehearsal clinic before the showcase. On stage, you have six minutes to pitch and four minutes to answer questions about pricing, distribution, competition and responsible execution. Judges score customer insight, feasibility, differentiation and the strength of your next experiment. Every finalist leaves with written feedback and a realistic action plan; prize funding is a fictional, one-time cash award with no equity attached. Bring your prototype, cost assumptions and a team member ready to explain what your interviews changed.

4a8ba284-612f-545b-be1d-0e271cc97657.name: Unmuted: Student Slam Poetry
4a8ba284-612f-545b-be1d-0e271cc97657.blurb: Four minutes, your own words and a room ready to listen.
4a8ba284-612f-545b-be1d-0e271cc97657.description:
Unmuted gives student writers a microphone and a clear invitation: say something you have been working to say. Poems may move through a hometown memory, an absurd hostel incident, an argument with yourself or a question the classroom leaves unanswered. The performance is built around original words and the human voice, with no backing track, costume change or prop required to make a poem land.

The first round welcomes twenty-eight poets, each with a four-minute piece in English, Hindi, Marathi or a mix of languages. Six finalists return with a second poem after a short break. The host introduces a simple listening agreement so the room remains attentive without becoming solemn; applause is welcome, interruptions are not. You can request a brief microphone check and choose to read from a page. Bring two completed pieces if you want to compete for the final, and expect a programme where tenderness, wit and a surprising line can all find their place.

9a5c1819-17d6-5492-bac7-44d80df98f63.name: Earth in Your Hands: Pinch-Pot Studio
9a5c1819-17d6-5492-bac7-44d80df98f63.blurb: Shape a small bowl in clay, experiment with texture and leave with a calmer approach to making by hand.
9a5c1819-17d6-5492-bac7-44d80df98f63.description:
Take a break from screens and learn what a small lump of clay can become with careful pressure and patience. This beginner studio teaches pinch-pot construction through a shallow bowl or ring dish. You will learn to keep the wall thickness even, smooth a rim without collapsing the form and add surface texture using simple stamps. The facilitator demonstrates how clay changes as it dries, so you understand why a rushed join cracks and why an elegant thin edge may not survive handling.

The final hour is devoted to a quiet finishing session and a short group conversation about form, balance and everyday use. Your piece is labelled and left with the studio for drying and firing; it is not ready to take home on the same day. One basic transparent glaze and the first firing are included, with collection planned three weeks later. The session welcomes complete beginners and offers a seated workstation option. Wear clothes that can handle a little clay and come prepared to enjoy making one thoughtful object rather than several hurried ones.

d10fc80a-b1dc-56f3-9e21-37ee22f0d98b.name: Ampersand: Battle of the Bands
d10fc80a-b1dc-56f3-9e21-37ee22f0d98b.blurb: Build a twelve-minute set that makes the whole amphitheatre sing back.
d10fc80a-b1dc-56f3-9e21-37ee22f0d98b.description:
Ampersand puts the campus stage in the hands of live student bands, from indie rock quartets to folk-fusion collectives and horn-led funk crews. Each shortlisted act gets twelve minutes to tell a musical story: an original, a daring rearrangement, or a set that moves confidently between both. Judges listen for ensemble balance, musical choices and the way you draw an audience into the performance, rather than simply rewarding the loudest guitar solo.

The evening begins with scheduled line checks so you can settle your levels before the audience arrives. A shared drum kit, keyboard stand and stage monitors are available, while bands bring their own instruments and pedalboards. Between competitive sets, the host introduces the people behind the songs and keeps changeovers moving. Submit a rehearsal recording with your registration, plan a set that fits the clock, and leave space for the moment when a hundred voices join your chorus.

1b87d482-b95f-519d-9bb7-1a5c5e95a954.name: AccessFirst: The Inclusive Interface Sprint
1b87d482-b95f-519d-9bb7-1a5c5e95a954.blurb: Redesign a campus service around keyboard access, clear language and real usability evidence.
1b87d482-b95f-519d-9bb7-1a5c5e95a954.description:
AccessFirst asks design teams to make a campus service easier for people who are usually left out of the first draft. The brief presents a fictional library booking flow with confusing labels, weak contrast and mouse-only interactions. Your team will map the barriers, choose a focused user journey and prototype a clearer alternative. Visual polish matters, but the jury will also inspect keyboard behaviour, error messages, touch targets and the reasoning behind each design decision.

The one-day sprint combines a short accessibility orientation with independent design time and two guided critique stops. Volunteer testers will try your key flow using a supplied checklist; you will record what failed, revise the prototype and explain the trade-offs in a concise handoff. Code is optional: an annotated interactive design prototype is eligible if it demonstrates focus order and intended semantics. Students from design, engineering, humanities and other disciplines can contribute by interviewing, writing, prototyping or testing. You will leave with a sharper case study and concrete feedback on a product experience rather than another isolated screen mock-up.

1c991a44-7b75-5396-84f3-59f924d11fe4.name: Nritya Rekha: Classical Solo Showcase
1c991a44-7b75-5396-84f3-59f924d11fe4.blurb: Tell a story through rhythm, expression and the discipline of a classical solo.
1c991a44-7b75-5396-84f3-59f924d11fe4.description:
Nritya Rekha offers Bharatanatyam and Kathak dancers a quiet, attentive stage for a complete solo presentation. Bring an item that reflects your training and your own interpretation: a rhythmic piece with precise footwork, an expressive passage that develops a character, or a thoughtful blend of both within one classical form. The jury considers technique alongside abhinaya, musical understanding and the way a dancer sustains a coherent performance.

Each participant introduces the composition, poet or theme in a short spoken note before a six-to-eight-minute solo. The studio theatre has a level wooden floor, a dressing area and a carefully managed playback desk; there is no expectation of an elaborate set or expensive costume. A shared opening session introduces the judging approach, and performers receive individual comments at the end. Whether you are preparing for your first college-stage appearance or refining a repertoire item, the showcase offers a respectful audience and clear feedback without rushing the expressive moments that make classical dance memorable.

50f647f3-367c-5bac-bcbe-c9e63a072f3d.name: Lightwear: Arduino Wearable Studio
50f647f3-367c-5bac-bcbe-c9e63a072f3d.blurb: Make a motion-responsive LED wristband and learn the wiring, code and safety habits behind wearable electronics.
50f647f3-367c-5bac-bcbe-c9e63a072f3d.description:
Turn a simple wristband into a small piece of responsive stagecraft. In Lightwear, pairs build a battery-powered wearable using an Arduino-compatible controller, an accelerometer and a short strip of addressable LEDs. You will first test each component on a breadboard, then write a sketch that changes colour patterns when the wearer moves. The design challenge is to make the effect readable from a few metres away while keeping the device comfortable, lightweight and easy to switch off.

The facilitator guides you through current limits, insulated connections and strain relief before you mount the circuit on a fabric cuff. Shared soldering stations are supervised, and a solder-free assembly route is available for beginners. Each pair takes home one completed prototype and a wiring diagram that makes future repairs possible. This is a learning build rather than a certified consumer product: the final check looks for secure batteries, covered conductors and sensible brightness. Bring curiosity, closed-toe shoes and a partner who enjoys making things work as much as making them look good.

f7cc220d-8035-57a5-9821-aa6fc7635fcb.name: Access by Design: Inclusive App Workshop
f7cc220d-8035-57a5-9821-aa6fc7635fcb.blurb: Audit a sample app with a keyboard and screen reader, then repair the barriers in a small web form.
f7cc220d-8035-57a5-9821-aa6fc7635fcb.description:
A beautiful interface can still shut people out when labels are missing, focus disappears or an error is communicated only by colour. This live online workshop uses a fictional scholarship application to make those barriers visible. You will navigate the form without a mouse, inspect its reading order and listen to a short screen-reader demonstration before looking at the underlying HTML. The facilitator shows how semantic controls, clear instructions and predictable focus help users who rely on assistive technology as well as people working under temporary constraints.

You will then repair a small starter page and compare the behaviour before and after the change. Exercises cover names and labels, validation messages, modal focus and reduced-motion preferences; automated checks are used as clues rather than a complete verdict. The final peer review asks each participant to describe an observed barrier and demonstrate the fix. This free session includes a recording and an accessible checklist, with captions enabled during the live teaching. Bring basic HTML familiarity and a willingness to test the experience instead of relying only on a score.

a6de479e-c82e-567a-a7a8-61207e455385.blurb: Follow clues across web security, forensics, cryptography and reverse engineering in a safe sandbox.
a6de479e-c82e-567a-a7a8-61207e455385.description:
FlagHorizon is a jeopardy-style capture-the-flag contest where curiosity beats guesswork. Teams explore intentionally vulnerable web applications, inspect suspicious files, untangle small cryptographic puzzles and reverse engineer toy binaries to recover hidden flags. The challenge board starts with beginner routes and branches into harder chains, so a well-coordinated team can divide the work without needing every member to be an expert. All targets belong to an isolated event sandbox; real campus systems are never part of the game.

The six-hour online round includes a briefing on authorized testing and a live support channel for infrastructure issues. Dynamic scoring keeps popular challenges from dominating the table, while optional hints carry a visible points cost. At the finish, leading teams submit short write-ups explaining how they found their flags, then join a review call before prizes are confirmed. Bring a patient approach, clear notes and a willingness to teach teammates what you discover. This is a practical security puzzle day, with strict scope boundaries and space for both first-time solvers and experienced CTF players.

e63f2307-8b6f-575e-af50-8ab4fe2e3203.blurb: Reimagine an Indian street-food favourite with careful flavour, clean prep and a clear story.
e63f2307-8b6f-575e-af50-8ab4fe2e3203.description:
Gully Gourmet challenges student cooks to take one familiar Indian street-food dish and give it a considered new direction without losing the pleasure that made it a favourite. A team might rethink misal toppings, balance a millet chaat or build a regional filling into a neatly portioned roll. The brief rewards flavour and texture first, then practical service, food handling and a convincing explanation of what you changed.

Each team receives a shared-standard induction station and a limited pantry of staples, while bringing declared fresh ingredients and a tested recipe. You have ninety minutes to prepare eight tasting portions for the jury; this is a judged cookoff, not a public food sale. A kitchen briefing covers handwashing, temperature control and allergen labels before cooking begins. All twelve stations are booked, so this page now supports registered teams preparing their menus. Plan a dish that can be finished on induction heat, served safely and described with pride in a two-minute conversation.

757a47ab-3e29-5ed2-936a-87cff1b818a2.description:
One round starts with a familiar soundtrack; the next asks you to connect a film poster, a cricket celebration and a phrase that took over the internet. This quiz explores Indian popular culture across languages and decades, from cinema and television to music, sport, advertising and online communities. The question set rewards recognising a story and making a connection rather than memorising release dates. Expect visual clues, short audio clips and a few answers that become obvious only after your teammate notices a tiny detail.

Teams of two or three begin with a written preliminary round, and the top eight move to the stage final. Finalists face pounce-and-bounce questions, a themed connection round and a fast written closer, with the scoring method explained before each segment. Audio and visual clues are also described where practical so the room can follow the reveal. The atmosphere is competitive but friendly: audience members get their own unscored questions while scores are checked. Gather teammates whose interests differ, keep your phones away during play and prepare to discover the wonderfully strange links in everyday entertainment.

Yes, And is a theatre competition for teams who can listen as quickly as they speak. Instead of memorised scripts, you will work with fresh prompts supplied at the event: an unlikely location, a relationship under pressure or an ordinary task that suddenly becomes complicated. The strongest scenes make partners look good, establish a clear situation and develop it together, rather than stacking one-liners until the story disappears.

Every team plays three short-form games in the preliminary round, with an experienced student host explaining each format before the clock starts. The top four return for a longer scene built from an audience suggestion and one surprise constraint. A short opening warm-up lets first-time performers practise accepting an offer and entering a scene with purpose. There are no costumes or sets to carry, but there is plenty to prepare: trust, shared habits and the willingness to let a teammate’s unexpected choice change where the scene goes.

da4774c1-0acb-5caa-a7be-e875e2cc120e.blurb: Learn to navigate the November sky, keep an observing log and take your first look through a telescope.
da4774c1-0acb-5caa-a7be-e875e2cc120e.description:
SkyLedger invites you to slow down and read the night sky from the campus observatory terrace. Student astronomy guides will introduce a seasonal sky map, show how to find bright reference stars and help you record what you actually see in a small observing log. Telescope targets will be chosen on the night according to visibility, weather and safe equipment alignment; the programme prioritizes good observing habits over a promise of a particular planet or dramatic photograph.

Participants rotate through a naked-eye orientation, a binocular station and two supervised telescope stations, with time to compare notes and ask how astronomers distinguish observation from inference. A short session indoors explains light pollution, telescope magnification and why a fuzzy patch can be scientifically interesting. No prior astronomy knowledge or personal equipment is needed. Bring a light layer, comfortable shoes and curiosity, and keep your phone screen dim to protect the group’s night vision. If clouds prevent outdoor viewing, the event continues in the adjoining seminar room with a sky-navigation simulation, telescope demonstration and a guided reading of archival astronomical images.
